title: The Buddha Lies Down
hookLine: a late night of teaching, an aching back, and the Buddha lying down in the middle of it
carry: the lion's posture: rest inside the work, then rise
tomorrow: an old man, sick and tired. what line sent him home glowing?

lines: A NAP THAT FEELS LIKE QUITTING.
A FULL HALL, DEEP IN THE NIGHT.
MY BACK ACHES. I'LL LIE DOWN.
cards: A nap at four in the afternoon can feel like a confession: I quit early, I'm lazy, everyone else is still going. Now a hall, newly built, full of people who have come to hear the Buddha.
He has been teaching them deep into the night. The lamps are burning, the crowd is still listening, and the Buddha turns to his attendant Ananda and says: my back is aching. I'm going to stretch it.
In front of everyone, in the middle of the evening, the teacher lies down.

teach.b: Watch how he does it, because the sutta takes care to tell us. Before he lies down he asks Ananda to teach the gathering in his place, so the work goes on.
Then he folds his robe, lies on his right side in what the texts call the lion's posture, one foot resting on the other, mindful and clearly aware, with the thought of getting up again in mind.
Ananda teaches the path of one in training. And when he's done, the Buddha gets up and tells him: good, Ananda, good. That small scene holds a lot.
The Buddha doesn't apologize for his back. He doesn't push through until he collapses, and he doesn't drop the whole evening either.
He rests inside the work, on purpose, and he trusts someone else to carry it for a while. That's the difference between rest and quitting. Quitting walks away from the work.
Rest stays near it, lies down mindfully, and keeps the thought of rising.

The Buddhist path names right effort as one of its eight parts, and right effort, in this picture, includes a body that gets to stop. Even a teacher whose whole life was effort lay down when his back ached.
Here's a detail to tell someone tonight: in the suttas, the lion's posture is how the Buddha lies down to rest, mindful, with the intention to rise.

how: Monastics in many Buddhist traditions are taught to lie down mindfully in the lion's posture, on the right side, noting the intention to rise; lay practitioners sometimes use the same posture for rest.

o: giving up on a hard task for good
sleeping as long as the body wants, every day
stopping on purpose inside the work, meaning to rise

games.q: the night in the hall — tap the pairs.
p: lay down when his back ached
taught the gathering in his place
on the right side, one foot on the other
what he kept in mind as he rested

s: the Buddha always taught straight through the night without a break
in this sutta he lay down when his back ached and Ananda taught.
the Buddha lay down mindfully, with the thought of getting up
rest with the intention to rise, in the lion's posture.
resting means giving up on effort
rest stays near the work; quitting walks away from it.

games.q: you're helping run a school fundraiser and your head is pounding. a friend offers to take over the table for an hour. what fits the story?
o: refuse; leaders don't stop until it's over.
go home and drop the whole event.
hand her the table, rest nearby, and come back.
games.why: the Buddha asked Ananda to teach, lay down mindfully, and rose again to praise him. rest inside the work, not out of it.

practice: Sit back, or lie down if you can, and let the shoulders drop. Let the hands rest open, the belly soften and the jaw go loose, the way the Buddha let his back stretch out.
Rest on purpose, without guilt, knowing you will get up again when the sit ends.

wordCard.voice: Rest: lying down mindfully inside the work, with the intention to rise, as the Buddha did when his back ached.

orig.note: Pali: sihaseyya, the lion's posture for lying down.

carryVoice: One line to keep: the lion's posture. Rest inside the work, mindful, with the thought of rising. Two of nine.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 53 (Sekha Sutta: after teaching the Sakyans late into the night, the Buddha says his back is uncomfortable, asks Ananda to teach, and lies down in the lion's posture, mindful, noting the time to rise; afterward he approves Ananda's teaching)
